subtitle: How a Song of the Motherland Stirred a Nation and Split Its Conscience

panels.shot: dramatic three-quarter view, mid-shot of Bankim seated at a desk, pages of a manuscript swirling around him as a ghostly map of Bengal and crowds of protesters fade in behind
panels.action: Bankim Chandra Chatterjee sits at a wooden desk with a quill paused in hand, his thoughtful gaze lifted as behind him, in misty suggestion, rise the outlines of Anandamath’s sanyasis, British officers, and mass processions clutching flags.

dialogue.text: From a deputy magistrate’s pen in Bengal came ‘Vande Mataram’—a song that fired freedom’s imagination, yet left India arguing over whose mother it praised.

i18n.hi: बंगाल के एक डिप्टी मजिस्ट्रेट की कलम से निकला ‘वंदे मातरम्’ – आज़ादी के सपनों को आग देने वाला गीत, पर बहस भी कि ये किसकी माँ की बात करता है

panels.shot: slow push-in on young Bankim in a Calcutta University hall, low-angle to suggest rising talent
panels.action: A young Bankim Chandra in traditional attire stands among a small group of students in a high-ceilinged Calcutta University hall, clutching a certificate as British professors look on from a dais.

dialogue.text: In the 1860s, as Calcutta University minted its first graduates, Bankim Chandra stepped out—Bengali, Hindu, English-educated, and already wrestling with the empire that now schooled him.

i18n.hi: 1860 के दशक में, जब कलकत्ता यूनिवर्सिटी ने पहले ग्रेजुएट निकाले, बंकिमचंद्र निकले बाहर – बंगाली, हिंदू, अंग्रेज़ी-पढ़ा, और उस राज से ही जूझते जो अब उसे पढ़ा रहा था

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder shot of Bankim in a colonial courtroom, looking from the judge’s bench to the people
panels.action: Bankim Chandra, now older and in a deputy magistrate’s seat, presides over a modest colonial courtroom, British insignia behind him while villagers await judgement on one side and a European officer confers with a clerk on the other.

dialogue.text: As a deputy magistrate of the Raj, he wore the crown’s authority; yet at night he turned to fiction, seeking a language where Bengal, not Britain, held the centre.

i18n.hi: राज के डिप्टी मजिस्ट्रेट के रूप में वह ताज की ताकत पहनता, पर रातों में वह कहानीकार बन जाता, ऐसी ज़बान खोजते हुए जहाँ केंद्र में बंगाल हो, ब्रिटेन नहीं

panels.shot: wide shot of Bankim at home at night, lamplight, manuscripts scattered; family asleep in the background
panels.action: In a dimly lit room, Bankim Chandra sits cross-legged by an oil lamp, manuscripts of Durgeshnandini and other early novels spread around, while in the background his household sleeps behind a curtain.

dialogue.text: Durgeshnandini and other tales poured from his hand, birthing the modern Bengali novel, even as he insisted that British rule had brought order to a once-fractured land.

i18n.hi: दुर्गेशनंदिनी जैसी कहानियाँ उमड़ पड़ीं, आधुनिक बंगाली उपन्यास जन्मा, और साथ ही वह दोहराता रहा कि अंग्रेज़ी राज ने बिखरी धरती में क़ायदा लौटाया

panels.shot: close-up on Bankim’s face as he pauses mid-writing, eyes distant, hearing inner music
panels.action: A close view shows Bankim Chandra frozen mid-stroke over a fresh page, his eyes lifted as if listening, the shadows of waving trees outside playing over his face.

dialogue.text: Somewhere between 1875 and 1882, a new cadence came to him—a hymn to the land itself, neither sermon nor slogan yet, but a whisper: Vande Mataram.

i18n.hi: 1875 और 1882 के बीच कहीं, एक नई लय आई – धरती के नाम एक भजन, न पूरा नारा, न उपदेश, बस धीमी फुसफुसाहट: वंदे मातरम्

panels.shot: top-down view of a manuscript page as Bankim writes the first two stanzas, his hand steady
panels.action: Bankim’s hand, steady and deliberate, inscribes neat Bengali lines on a fresh sheet, the words ‘Vande Mataram’ beginning a stanza as his inkpot and quill rest beside.

dialogue.text: He wrote of the motherland in simple, lush images—green fields, cool winds, clear waters—verses that offered a tender, almost devotional love without yet naming a god.

i18n.hi: उसने मातृभूमि को सादी, हरी-भरी तस्वीरों में गाया – खेत, ठंडी हवा, साफ़ पानी – ऐसी पंक्तियाँ जिनमें कोमल, भक्ति जैसी ममता थी, बिना किसी देवता का नाम लिए

panels.shot: pull-back to reveal a second manuscript where the later, goddess-rich stanzas appear beside the first
panels.action: The view widens to show another page where Bankim’s script flows into later verses, filled with metaphors of Durga-like forms, halos and weapons pencilled faintly in the margin by his own hand.

dialogue.text: Then the tone deepened. Later stanzas hailed the mother as goddess, sword-bearing and many-armed, folding Hindu imagery into the same song that had begun as an ode to the land.

i18n.hi: फिर सुर बदला। आगे के अंतरों में माँ देवी बनी – तलवारदार, बहु-बाहु – वही गीत अब धरती के साथ हिंदू रूपकों से भर गया

panels.shot: medium shot of Bankim discussing a manuscript with a conservative Bengali gentleman in a drawing room
panels.action: In a genteel Calcutta drawing room, Bankim Chandra leans forward, manuscript of Anandamath in hand, as a bearded Bengali gentleman in traditional dress listens with furrowed brow amidst shelves of books.

dialogue.speaker: bankim_chandra_chatterjee
dialogue.text: Our people must imagine themselves again—not as subjects, but as children of this soil.

i18n.hi: हमारी क़ौम को खुद को फिर देखना होगा – प्रजा नहीं, इस मिट्टी की औलाद बनकर

panels.shot: dramatic illustration-within-the-panel: Anandamath’s imagined sanyasis in a stormy landscape contrasted with a calm Bankim writing
panels.action: Half the panel shows Bankim quietly writing at his desk; the other half depicts his imagined world—robed sanyasi warriors striding through a storm-darkened Bengal countryside, ruined villages behind them.

dialogue.text: In 1882, Anandamath appeared, set in the famine-ravaged 1770s, with ascetic warriors rising against rule they saw as alien, and with ‘Vande Mataram’ woven through their march.

i18n.hi: 1882 में ‘आनंदमठ’ आया – 1770 के अकाल में बसा, जहाँ संन्यासी योद्धा उस राज के ख़िलाफ़ उठते हैं जिसे वे पराया मानते हैं, और उनकी चाल में ‘वंदे मातरम्’ गुंथा है

panels.shot: wide shot of a fictional scene: Anandamath’s sanyasis confronting Muslim soldiers, rendered like an illustration hovering behind Bankim
panels.action: Behind a reflective Bankim Chandra, a translucent tableau shows Anandamath’s sanyasis standing firm with staffs and swords against a line of turbaned Muslim soldiers guarding a fort, the landscape dry and stark.

dialogue.text: In its pages, Muslim rulers appear as oppressors—an imagined, sharpened conflict that mirrored some memories of Mughal decline, yet also carved new communal lines into popular storytelling.

i18n.hi: इन पन्नों में मुस्लिम हाकिम ज़ालिम बनकर आते हैं – मुगल गिरावट की कुछ यादों से जन्मा, पर नई सांप्रदायिक धारियाँ भी खींचता हुआ किस्सा

panels.shot: intimate close-up of Bankim closing the finished manuscript of Anandamath, half his face in shadow
panels.action: Bankim gently closes the bound manuscript of Anandamath, his face half-lit by lamplight, half in shadow, his expression unreadable as he holds the work with both hands.

dialogue.text: Bankim did not call for immediate independence; he still spoke of British rule as lawful. Yet in fiction he bestowed the highest devotion not on queen or crown, but on a sanctified motherland.

i18n.hi: बंकिम ने तुरंत आज़ादी नहीं माँगी; अंग्रेज़ी राज को वह अब भी क़ानूनी कहता रहा। पर कहानी में उसकी सर्वोच्च भक्ति रानी या ताज को नहीं, पवित्र की गई मातृभूमि को मिली

panels.shot: wide shot of a public reading in Bengal, with listeners rapt as a reader recites from Anandamath
panels.action: In a crowded courtyard, a reader stands on a low platform, Anandamath in hand, as men and women sit and stand in rapt attention, some eyes closed as they listen.

dialogue.text: The story travelled far beyond his study. Public readings, cheap editions, and retellings made its sanyasis and their song part of the new nationalist imagination in Bengal.

i18n.hi: कहानी उसकी मेज़ से बहुत दूर निकल गई। पाठ, सस्ते संस्करण, दोहराव – उससे संन्यासी और उनका गीत बंगाल की नई राष्ट्रीय कल्पना का हिस्सा बन गए

panels.shot: wide shot of the 1896 Congress session stage, with Rabindranath Tagore singing to an attentive audience
panels.action: On a large meeting stage in the 1890s, Rabindranath Tagore stands with harmonium, singing to rows of seated delegates under punkahs, with a banner of the Indian National Congress hanging above.

dialogue.text: In 1896, at an Indian National Congress session, Rabindranath Tagore set ‘Vande Mataram’ to music, his voice carrying the hymn into the formal politics of an awakening nation.

i18n.hi: 1896 में कांग्रेस के अधिवेशन में, रवींद्रनाथ टैगोर ने ‘वंदे मातरम्’ को धुन दी, उसकी आवाज़ ने इस भजन को जागती क़ौम की औपचारिक राजनीति तक पहुँचा दिया

panels.shot: montage-like wide shot of Swadeshi-era processions, banners raised, mouths open in song
panels.action: A broad street in early twentieth-century Bengal throngs with Swadeshi protesters, men and women marching, some holding spinning wheels and boycotting British cloth, their mouths wide as they sing together.

dialogue.text: Through the Swadeshi movement, its refrain echoed in marches, bonfires of foreign cloth, and secret gatherings; it became a national song long before there was a nation-state to claim it.

i18n.hi: स्वदेशी आंदोलन में इसका साज़ हर क़दम पर गूँजा – जुलूसों में, विदेशी कपड़ों की होलियों में, गुप्त बैठकों में; राष्ट्र बनने से पहले ही यह राष्ट्रीय गीत बन बैठा

panels.shot: medium shot of a Muslim political gathering, leaders in discussion, a few frowning at mention of the song
panels.action: In a modest hall, Muslim leaders sit in discussion, some in sherwanis and caps, one gesturing as others listen; a couple of faces show concern as a paper with ‘Vande Mataram’ written in Urdu lies on the table.

dialogue.text: Yet for many Muslims, the song’s later verses and Anandamath’s narrative stung—the motherland hailed as a Hindu goddess, their rulers cast as the enemy, their place in the imagined nation left uncertain.

i18n.hi: पर कई मुसलमानों के लिए बाद के अंतरे और ‘आनंदमठ’ की कहानी चुभी – मातृभूमि को हिंदू देवी, उनके शासकों को दुश्मन, और कल्पित राष्ट्र में उनका स्थान धुँधला

panels.shot: intercut shot: one side Hindu students singing fervently; other side Muslim students standing silent, uneasy
panels.action: One side of the panel shows Hindu students in a school courtyard singing with hands raised; the other side shows a group of Muslim students nearby, standing quietly, some looking away, one with arms folded.

dialogue.text: In schools and meetings, the same refrain that thrilled some hearts left others quiet, or absent; the song that had united many also began to mark a line.

i18n.hi: स्कूलों और बैठकों में, वही धुन जो कुछ दिलों को जोश देती थी, कुछ को ख़ामोश, या ग़ाइब छोड़ जाती; जो गीत जोड़ता था, वही एक रेखा भी खींचने लगा

panels.shot: interior of a Congress Working Committee meeting in 1937, leaders seated around a long table, documents before them
panels.action: A long table is ringed by Indian National Congress leaders in khadi, pens and papers before them, as one elder member points to a resolution draft while others listen with grave attention.

dialogue.text: By 1937, the Congress Working Committee faced the dilemma openly. They debated a resolution on ‘Vande Mataram’—how to honour a beloved song without deepening the division it now symbolised.

i18n.hi: 1937 तक, कांग्रेस वर्किंग कमेटी को सीधे इस उलझन से भिड़ना पड़ा। उन्होंने ‘वंदे मातरम्’ पर प्रस्ताव पर बहस की – प्यारे गीत का मान कैसे रखो, बिना उस दरार को गहरा किए जिसे वह दिखाता था

panels.shot: close-up of the resolution document, the line about only using the first two stanzas highlighted by light
panels.action: A hand smooths a typed resolution on a wooden desk, the clause specifying that only the first two stanzas be used in public sessions catching a shaft of light from a nearby window.

dialogue.text: Their October 1937 resolution drew a careful line: in public, only the first two stanzas—those of fields, forests and loving praise—would be sung; the goddess-rich verses stayed outside official ceremonies.

i18n.hi: अक्टूबर 1937 के उनके प्रस्ताव ने एक नाज़ुक रेखा खींची: मंच पर सिर्फ़ पहले दो अंतरे – खेत, जंगल और प्यार का गुणगान – गाए जाएँ; देवी-भरे हिस्से सरकारी रस्मों से बाहर रहें

panels.shot: symbolic wide shot: two stages side by side, one with Jana Gana Mana being sung, the other with Vande Mataram, audiences overlapping
panels.action: A symbolic scene shows two adjacent stages: on one, singers perform ‘Jana Gana Mana’; on the other, a group sings ‘Vande Mataram’, while in the crowd between them people move, some turning to one stage, some to the other.

dialogue.text: Later, another song would be chosen as anthem, while ‘Vande Mataram’ remained a national song—honoured, contested, cherished by many, questioned by others, never quite slipping into quiet.

i18n.hi: बाद में एक और गीत राष्ट्रगान बना, और ‘वंदे मातरम्’ राष्ट्रीय गीत – सम्मानित, विवादित, कई के लिए प्यारा, कुछ के लिए सवालों से भरा, कभी पूरी तरह चुप न हुआ

panels.shot: soft-focus shot of an older Bankim in his final years, seated with a book in hand, oblivious to the future debates
panels.action: An older Bankim Chandra sits in a simple chair, wrapped in a shawl, a copy of Anandamath resting on his lap as he gazes out of a window, unaware of the restless crowds his words will one day summon.

dialogue.text: Bankim died in 1894, before swadeshi fires, before Congress resolutions; he never saw how his careful loyalty to the Raj and his fervent love for the motherland would collide in later minds.

i18n.hi: बंकिम 1894 में चले गए – स्वदेशी की आग से पहले, कांग्रेस के फैसलों से पहले; उसने नहीं देखा कि राज के प्रति उसकी सावधान वफ़ादारी और मातृभूमि के लिए उसका जज़्बा बाद की सोच में कैसे टकराएगा

panels.shot: final wide shot: contemporary India in silhouette, diverse people standing under a vast sky, Bankim’s faint figure and manuscript in the clouds above
panels.action: Under a vast dusk sky, a diverse crowd of Indians—different faiths and dress—stand in silhouette across a landscape, while high above them, faint like a clouded watermark, hover the figure of Bankim and a page bearing the words ‘Vande Mataram’.

dialogue.text: Today, each time the song is sung or questioned, it recalls Bankim’s troubled gift—a reminder that the words which rouse a people can also force them to ask who is included in their ‘we’.

i18n.hi: आज, जब भी गीत गाया या पूछा जाता है, वह बंकिम की उलझी सौगात याद दिलाता है – कि जो शब्द लोगों को जगाते हैं, वही यह सवाल भी उठाते हैं कि हमारे ‘हम’ में कौन-कौन है

title_i18n.hi: वंदे मातरम् का जन्म, तूफ़ानी शुरुआत

subtitle_i18n.en: How a Song of the Motherland Stirred a Nation and Split Its Conscience
subtitle_i18n.hi: मातृभूमि के गीत ने देश जगाया, ज़मीर को दो हिस्सों में बाँट दिया
